items.title: Solid 2.0
items.summary: javascript, web
items.content:
5 years is a long time to work on anything. It took 5 years from my first commit of Solid to 1.0, and it's been another 5 since then. A lot changes in 5 years. Solid 1.0 made a bet that fine-grained reactivity, signals, was the right foundation for building user interfaces. Back then it was an unusual position. Today signals are everywhere. In Angular, in Svelte's runes, in Vue Vapor, and in a proposal before TC39 to put them in the language itself. It even pushed the conversation into React's compiler. More recently that conversation has shifted to AI, arguably an even larger change in how we build. But Solid has always been about building the right things; the performant things. So for us the mission hasn't really changed all that much. The things that we identified as standout about our approach still stand out now. But instead of living in the shadow of more popular solutions Solid 2.0 carves out a path that others can follow. Deliberately this time. If fine-grained reactivity's greatest strength is knowing the shape of our application, that knowledge shouldn't end with the process, or the machine the code is running on. Real applications are distributed. Real applications are born from data that lives on a server. The coordination of these pieces should be intentional and by design. This starts with bringing async into the graph. A computation can return a Promise or an async iterator, and everything downstream just understands: const user = createMemo (() => fetchUser (props.id)); < h1 class = {{ stale : isPending (user) }} > { user ().name} fetchUser(props.id)); return ( }>

{user().name}

  );}"> This allows authoring by affordance while automating the handling of race conditions. The introduction of async doesn't cause an app refactor. Speculative state is automatically rolled back without manually written processes ensuring the server remains the authority on truth. SolidStart introduce the world to server functions in early 2022, and now they have found their way home to Solid's core, better than ever. Not only do they support highly capable RPC calls over Request/Response but persistent connections over Server Sent Events. And consuming it remains as simple as the code below. import { live } from "@solidjs/web/server-functions" ; const stockPrice = live ( async function* ( symbol : string ) { for await ( const tick of subscribe (symbol)) yield tick.price; const price = createMemo (() => stockPrice ()) This is only the beginning of what can be done with Server Functions and we will be announcing some new features (like reactive Server Components) in coming weeks that leverage this capability. "But, we aren't writing the code anymore!" We hear you. A system built on constraints by construction ends up with less code to maintain and less edge cases. What used to be considered a DX shortcoming of reactive frameworks are now their greatest strength. And Solid 2.0 goes all in. Every framework now says it "works great with AI", and usually that means models have seen a lot of it. That's a statement about training data, not about the framework. The question that matters is what happens when the agent gets it wrong. In most frameworks a reactive mistake is silent. The app runs, it's just wrong, and the framework can't tell you, because it can't see it either. Solid can. A fine-grained graph knows exactly what was read, where, and what will update. So Solid 2.0's development builds report mistakes as they happen, with a stable code, the location in your source, and the fix: [STRICT_READ_UNTRACKED] Reactive value read directly in an effect callback will not update. items.content_ko: Solid 개발자는 Solid의 첫 커밋부터 1.0까지 5년, 그 이후로도 5년이 걸렸다고 회고한다. Solid 1.0은 세밀한 반응성, 즉 시그널이 UI 구축의 올바른 기반이라는 방향을 택했는데, 당시에는 드문 입장이었다. 지금은 시그널이 Angular, Svelte의 runes, Vue Vapor에서 쓰이고, TC39에는 시그널을 언어에 넣자는 제안도 올라와 있다. React 컴파일러에서도 이 논의가 이어졌다. 최근 업계의 관심은 AI로 옮겨 갔지만, Solid의 목표는 성능이 좋고 올바른 것을 만드는 일로 크게 바뀌지 않았다고 한다. Solid 2.0은 인기 있는 대안의 그늘에 머무르기보다 다른 이들이 따를 수 있는 길을 분명히 개척하는 것을 목표로 한다. 세밀한 반응성의 강점이 애플리케이션 구조에 대한 이해라면, 그 지식은 프로세스나 실행 기기에서 끝나서는 안 되며 실제 애플리케이션은 분산되어 있다는 점을 강조한다. (원문 일부만 제공됨)

items.title: HP Poly VoIP vulnerability sets the stage for executive voice deepfakes
items.content:
HP has released patches for a critical buffer overflow vulnerability in multiple IP-enabled conference phones from its Poly Voice line. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to obtain root privileges on the underlying operating system, potentially enabling them to execute other attacks such as eavesdropping on conversations and recording voice data for AI-enabled impersonation attacks.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-0826 , was discovered by researchers from security firm Rapid7 and resides in the code that parses Session Description Protocol (SDP) attributes when the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) feature is enabled.

ICE enables VoIP devices to establish peer-to-peer connections using the shortest available network path. The feature is not enabled by default on HP Poly devices, and the company advises administrators to disable it if it’s not needed.

The flaw, rated 9.2 on the CVSS severity scale, affects all phones from the HP Poly VVX series, as well as the Trio 8300, 8500, and 8800 IP conference devices. HP has fixed the flaw in its Poly Unified Communications Software (UCS) versions 6.4.8 for the VVX devices, 8.1.7 for the Trio 8300, and 7.2.8 for Trio 8500 and 8800.

An exploit module targeting this vulnerability has already been developed and released for the widely used Metasploit penetration testing framework that’s maintained by Rapid7.

The exploit executes code as root on an affected device with ICE enabled by sending a SIP INVITE request with a specially crafted candidate attribute. This attribute normally contains a transport address that can be used for connectivity checks and is part of the ICE RFC8839 standard.

The buffer overflow bug is located in a helper function called ParseICECandidate in the polyapp binary that processes such requests on the device.

“The start of the function contains a call to memcpy , which will copy the incoming string line being processed into a 256 byte stack buffer,” Stephen Fewer, senior principal security researcher at Rapid7, said in a blog post . “No length check is performed to ensure the incoming string length is less than 256 bytes. Therefore by providing a candidate attribute whose length is greater than 256 bytes, a stack-based buffer overflow will occur.”

Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), a kernel feature that randomizes memory addresses to defeat buffer overflow exploits, is enabled on the device. However, the protection is not operating correctly on the HP Poly devices because it does not randomize the load addresses of .so (Shared Object) libraries.

These libraries, such as libc , are loaded by other processes, including the polyapp process, and because their memory addresses never change, they can be leveraged to bypass ASLR and execute the attacker’s payload.

“We create a ROP chain that will execute an arbitrary OS command via the system standard C library function,” Fewer said. “The accompanying Metasploit exploit modules source code details the entire ROP chain.”

Attackers have increasingly targeted embedded devices inside enterprise networks in recent years because unlike laptops, workstations, and servers, these devices are not monitored by endpoint detection and response (EDR) products. As such, they provide perfect footholds inside corporate environments that allow attackers to remain undetected for long periods of time and attack other systems.

In the age of AI these devices become even more relevant for attackers, going beyond corporate espionage by recording conversations or internal network pivoting.

“Attackers no longer need massive datasets to make use of synthetic speech tooling,” Douglas McKee, Rapid7’s director of vulnerability intelligence, said in a blog post . “In many cases, they just need clean source audio of the right person saying enough words in enough contexts. That has made executive voice data, call recordings, and live conversation capture far more valuable than many organizations seem prepared…

items.title: Banks and the NSA Admit That Yes, It Was AI That Caused the Massive Outages: There's good news and there's bad news.
items.content:
It’s been an extraordinary month of outages causing major tech services to shut down — and we’re only just over half way through November.

The list is extensive: a nationwide ground halt shutting down all airfare in the US for hours, days without access to core Microsoft services including Outlook and Teams, Apple’s App Store and Apple Pay went down , US banks experienced major disruptions , and United Airlines had to delay and cancel countless flights after a major system outage. Even the National Security Agency’s in-house communications network for classified information went down earlier this week.

The massive outages — as well as a spate of wide-ranging hacks — have flummoxed lawmakers, who are now trying to get a better sense of what’s going on. According to early indications, widespread suspicions that AI may have played a role appear to be warranted, though there’s nuance in exactly how.

As the Washington Sun reports , Wall Street and National Security Agency sources have already told Congress that the outages are being triggered due to system updates designed to thwart future attacks by AI.

Put simply, the tech industry and federal government are attempting to bolster their defenses as AI continues to identify glaring cybersecurity vulnerabilities that could be exploited by bad actors. To implement these updates, it sounds like load-bearing organizations have inadvertently overwhelmed their systems, wreaking havoc with the online services we’ve grown heavily dependent on.

The news aligns with officials’ continued reassurances that the outages are not related to any cybersecurity threats. At the same time, the urgency with which power players are trying to shore up their systems raises the possibility that hackers could already be gearing up for their next offensive.

“These models are identifying massive vulnerabilities, and that increases the urgency to patch right away,” a congressional official told the Washington Sun . “They’re trying to push through a lot of patches all at once — more than the system was designed for.”

Department of Homeland Security secretary Markwayne Mullin similarly told reporters on Tuesday that “new technology” is being pushed “on top of really old computer systems,” which overwhelmed them.

“I can tell you 98 percent certainty this isn’t a cyberattack,” he added.

None of this is surprising to longtime observers. Experts have warned for years about AI being a dangerous double-edged sword: on one hand, it can give cybersecurity researchers a major leg up in identifying possible new attacks. (Earlier this year, Anthropic claimed in a report that its Claude Mythos model had found more than ten thousand vulnerabilities in existing software.)

On the other hand, hackers can use the same tools to exploit these vulnerabilities, setting the stage for an arms race we seemingly are in the midst of as companies are rushing to patch these defects.

It’s a precarious moment as both the federal government and the private tech industry are battening down the hatches at a fever pace, presumably fearing future outages that could indeed be caused by a cyberattack.

“There’s some sense in which this is reassuring, in that it means there’s not an attack,” Encode chief strategy officer Nathan Calvin told the Washington Sun . “But it shows the extent to which safety critical infrastructure we rely on is based on software with large vulnerabilities on legacy systems.”

To Calvin, it’s an arms race that will more than likely drag on “as we get more advanced models.”

items.title: Manage pairs around your text: mini.surround
items.content:
What do Neovim users do when they get bored? They rewrite their config file to optimize their startup time by saving 12 milliseconds. Then, they mess up with plugins and try new ones, just to break their config even more :)

just worked. So, why break what wasn’t broken? Why did I make the leap to

Grab a cup of your preferred Linux fuel, open up a terminal, and let’s talk about why this tiny module won over my heart, my config files, and my muscle memory.

mini.nvim is a collection of independent, hyper-focused, lightweight Lua modules written by a single mastermind (E. Chasnovski). By switching to mini.surround, I didn’t just replace a plugin, I opened the door to a unified suite. I’ll continue sharing my journey in the mini.nvim world through my “The Neovim mini collection” series.

Out of the box, nvim-surround mimics vim-surround using actions like ys , ds , and cs . It’s iconic, but it has a slight cognitive friction when you want to expand or query bindings.

mini.surround opts for a prefix-based structure ( sa for s urround a dd, sd for s urround d elete, sr for s urround r eplace).

Once your fingers adapt to the s prefix family, it maps neatly onto how you think about text manipulation: verb + target .

One of the subtle papercuts I experienced with nvim-surround was handling complex visual selections. When you highlight a multi-line block or a specific chunk of code and want to wrap it, behavior could occasionally require specific operator sequences.

mini.surround handles visual selections natively and gracefully. Highlight a chunk of code in visual mode, press sa followed by your delimiter, and boom your snippet is wrapped cleanly, respecting indentation rules right out of the box. It feels less like fighting an extension and more like an extension of Neovim’s core philosophy.

Moving away from nvim-surround wasn’t about the older plugin being bad, it’s phenomenal at what it does. But mini.surround gave me a faster, remarkably lean footprint with built-in search versatility and a cohesive ecosystem that aligns with a minimalist Linux workflow.

If you’re looking to trim down your init.lua without sacrificing a single ounce of text-editing power, give mini.surround a spin.

items.title: How I made a custom game engine for Satelital
items.summary: games, graphics
items.content:
For quite a long time, I've been working on a puzzle game called Satelital, a rule-discovery game about learning alien logic.

As a solo developer, I decided to start this project from scratch. My motivation was to learn the actual fundamentals behind the technology of videogames. This meant I had to build most of the tools I would need myself, including the game engine, renderer, puzzles, editors, UX, design, art and music.

Now that I've finally managed to release the game, I think it's a good moment to share how I built it.

The main reason I got into programming was the idea of eventually working on games. I spent many years working on web and building mobile apps. It was fun, but I felt like I wasn't going in the direction I really wanted to.

So one day, after listening to every Jonathan Blow talk I could find and playing too much The Witness, I decided to finally give it a try.

I spent many days and countless hours looking for the best tool I could use to make a game, but nothing left me satisfied. The closest I got to having fun with gamedev was with the LÖVE framework making a few jam games. But even with that, it felt quite limiting to not really know what was happening behind the graphics I somehow managed to animate on my screen.

I remember hearing about shaders and parallel programming. The concept always felt very arcane and mysterious to me, but now writing them is the thing I enjoy the most while coding.

I finally decided to jump into the swimming pool and actually learn C⁠+⁠+. I had to learn how to manage memory and how not to shoot myself in the foot with the wrong tools. I started using SDL2 while trying to use the C⁠+⁠+ standard library as little as possible.

Before getting too deep into the engine, I actually finished a prototype of the game quite early. It had very early versions of four kinds of puzzles that mostly survived until the final game. It was made entirely with SDL2, but I soon realised that if I wanted to have more interesting graphics, I would need to use shaders and decided to switch to OpenGL.

This puzzle was the first one I made, also the only one that survived until the end

With the help of LearnOpenGL I quickly had a triangle on the screen. From there, learning things like lighting, tonemapping, normal maps, shader effects and everything else opened up a whole new way of looking at computers for me. Before, my idea of how a computer actually draws to the screen was quite naive. When I started learning graphics I just wanted to be able to manually change the color of each pixel individually, but in the end the idea of running a program in parallel for every pixel clicked for me.

One thing that made a huge difference while working on shaders was having code reloading. Before that, I had a complex system that stored constant values in config files, which would later get passed through uniforms into shaders. Then a custom development menu would provide some UI to tweak those values at runtime. With that I stopped having to reload and compile everything for every little change I wanted to make.

It worked, but having to maintain all this extra scaffolding was slowing me down. Another unexpected downside of this setup was that, in some cases, the shader compiler couldn't optimize the code as well as it otherwise could, since knowing constant values ahead of time helps it make better decisions.

Having shader reloading made a huge difference. Being able to change some code, save the file and immediately see the result on screen was very useful. Iterating on shaders became much faster and more fun. This was probably my biggest regret about not having it from day one.

items.title: Hackers Are Using AI to Speed Through Cyberattacks, FBI Warns
items.content:
An open-source AI tool designed to find security flaws is helping hackers launch cyberattacks. The FBI says hackers are using Artex, an AI-powered security testing tool, to break into organizations worldwide. In an advisory on Friday , the agency said some attacks took less than 3 hours from selecting a target to gaining high-level access to its systems. Attackers have used Artex since at least August against banks, government agencies, technology companies and healthcare providers.

The advisory was issued the same day communications problems prompted a nationwide Federal Aviation Administration ground stop and a day after a major Microsoft 365 outage began. Microsoft attributed its disruption to technical problems, and the FAA says it has found no indication of a cyberattack.

An FBI official told ABC News ⁠ that Artex doesn’t appear to be connected to either incident or to other recent disruptions, including banking outages involving JPMorgan Chase .

The warning adds to concerns about the  security risks posed by AI agents , which can carry out tasks with little human supervision.

Artex automates security tests that organizations use to uncover weaknesses. According to  Microsoft’s analysis , its agents can examine defenses, exploit flaws and extract data. Attackers can use that automation to try several ways into a network simultaneously.

The FBI cited attacks against South Korean financial institutions that exposed the personal information of approximately 67,000 people. Microsoft warns that attackers breached over 2,250 organizations’ Microsoft 365 systems in a separate campaign, using stolen ConnectWise backup credentials alongside the Artex tool.

Because customers had already authorized the backup software, attackers could use its access without logging in as an individual user. Microsoft cautioned that a successful sign-in doesn’t necessarily mean data was accessed or stolen. The automated attacks could trigger security alerts, but their speed left defenders little time to respond.

This FBI Cyber advisory on ARTEX was released last Friday, 11/13. It is not a new announcement, and the FBI has not issued any additional warning since. The guidance in the advisory remains current.

We released this advisory last week because as we head to the end of the year,…

Amazon Web Services’ Nov. 13 research  described another scheme: Stealing credentials for AI services, and then using that access to hunt for more credentials at someone else’s expense. Amazon Threat Intelligence uncovered the activity through decoy systems posing as AI services. It linked the campaigns to Artex with moderate confidence but couldn’t independently verify results the agents reported on systems outside its monitoring.

Amazon said the attacks relied on default passwords, exposed login details and outdated software, all of which hackers can find and exploit faster with AI.

Artex’s developer removed the original GitHub repository in October after reports of abuse, but copies remain available, the FBI said. The agency recommends limiting access to sensitive systems, reviewing software permissions, replacing exposed credentials, and monitoring unusual account activity or large data transfers.

items.summary_ko: FBI는 해커들이 보안 취약점을 찾는 오픈소스 AI 도구 Artex를 악용해 전 세계 기관에 침투하고 있다고 경고했다. 일부 공격은 표적 선정부터 고권한 시스템 접근까지 3시간이 채 걸리지 않았고, 공격은 적어도 8월부터 은행, 정부기관, 기술 기업, 의료 기관을 겨냥해 이어졌다. FBI 관계자는 Artex가 최근의 FAA 운항 중단, Microsoft 365 장애, JPMorgan Chase 은행 장애와는 연관되어 보이지 않는다고 ABC News에 밝혔다.
items.content_ko: FBI는 금요일에 발표한 권고문에서, 보안 취약점을 찾기 위해 만들어진 오픈소스 AI 도구가 해커들의 사이버 공격에 쓰이고 있다고 밝혔다. 해커들은 AI 기반 보안 테스트 도구 Artex로 전 세계 조직에 침투하고 있으며, 일부 공격은 표적을 고른 뒤 3시간도 안 되어 고권한 시스템 접근까지 이루어졌다. 공격은 적어도 8월부터 이어졌고, 대상에는 은행, 정부기관, 기술 기업, 의료 기관이 포함된다. 이 권고문은 통신 문제로 FAA가 전국적 운항 중단(ground stop)을 내린 날 발표됐으며, Microsoft 365 대규모 장애가 시작된 다음 날이기도 했다. Microsoft는 장애 원인을 기술적 문제라고 설명했고, FAA는 사이버 공격의 징후를 찾지 못했다고 밝혔다. FBI 관계자는 Artex가 이 사건들이나 JPMorgan Chase 은행 장애 등 최근의 다른 장애와 관련된 것으로 보이지 않는다고 말했다. 이번 경고는 사람의 감독이 거의 없이 작업을 수행할 수 있는 AI 에이전트의 보안 위험에 대한 우려와도 맞닿아 있다. Artex는 조직들이 약점을 찾기 위해 쓰는 보안 테스트를 자동화하는 도구다. 매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.

items.summary_ko: Dokploy 0.31.0 이하 버전에서는 /etc/dokploy 디렉터리가 0777 권한으로 설정되어, 공유 호스트의 일반 사용자가 root 소유의 예약 작업 및 Traefik 설정 디렉터리를 바꿔치기할 수 있다. 이로 인해 바뀐 예약 작업 스크립트가 root 권한으로 실행될 수 있어 로컬 권한 상승으로 이어진다. 원문은 원격 악용 가능 여부를 False로 표기했고, CVSS 점수는 0.0(NA)으로 기재되어 있다.
items.content_ko: Dokploy는 자체 호스팅이 가능한 무료 PaaS(Platform as a Service)다. 이 취약점은 0.31.0 이하 버전에서 호스팅형 설치 프로그램과 수동 설치 안내가 /etc/dokploy 디렉터리를 0777 권한으로 설정하기 때문에 발생한다. 그 결과 공유 호스트에 있는 root가 아닌 로컬 사용자가 root 소유의 스케줄 설정이나 Traefik 설정 디렉터리를 다른 것으로 바꿔치기할 수 있다. Dokploy는 이 경로들을 신뢰할 수 있는 설정으로 사용하며, 바꿔치기된 예약 작업 스크립트를 root 권한으로 실행할 수 있다. 이로 인해 로컬 권한 상승이 일어난다. 원문에 따르면 CVSS 점수는 0.0(NA), 원격 악용 가능 여부는 False로 표기되어 있으며, 공개일은 2026-11-18이다.

items.title: The Cambridge Dictionary has named ‘human’ as the Word of the Year 2026
items.content:
The Cambridge Dictionary has named ‘human’ as the Word of the Year 2026.

The year has been defined by global debates on what it means to be human when AI is blurring the boundaries between people and machines.

'Human' is defined in the Cambridge Dictionary as ‘having the qualities, faults, and feelings that people have, as opposed to gods, animals, or machines’.

In 2026, many public figures defended humans and humanity in the age of AI. Bill Gates, Chair of the Gates Foundation, made the case for “human reserved jobs”, such as caregivers, that should never be taken by machines, in a widely read essay .

Commenting on the selection of ‘human’ as Cambridge Dictionary Word of the Year, he said: “AI is making us think harder about what it means to be human. It could help us cure diseases, improve education, and give people more time to spend on the things that matter most.

"But we need to make deliberate choices about how it fits into our lives, including where we want people to remain at the center. The measure of AI’s success should be how much it improves human lives.”

‘AI godfather’ and Nobel laureate Geoffrey Hinton has warned that “we’re creating alien beings. I’m willing to be selfish and choose humans.” And in his Magnifica Humanitas letter, Pope Leo XIV spoke of new forms of “dehumanization” and the “pressing duty to remain profoundly human”.

Actors Scarlett Johansson and Cate Blanchett, musicians Tayla Parx, LeAnn Rimes and Billie Eilish, and authors Jodi Picoult and Jonathan Franzen challenged an "assault on human creativity" as the Human Artistry Campaign and Artist Rights Alliance opposed machine-generated replicas and theft of human-generated content by large language models (LLMs).

Meanwhile, Project Hail Mary author Andy Weir has wondered whether he "might be among the last generation of fully human writers". The Authors Guild has launched a ‘Human Authored’ kitemark for books, supported by Professor Dame Mary Beard and Malorie Blackman.

As AI deepfakes simulated humans, Matthew McConaughey became the first Hollywood actor to pre-emptively protect himself against unauthorised digital reproduction by trademarking clips of his voice, his face and even his catchphrase ‘alright, alright, alright’.  Taylor Swift followed suit, trademarking her voice and image in April.

Professor Rachel Adams, an expert on AI governance and human rights at the University of Cambridge, said: “AI brings us back to questions that we’ve asked for millennia: who are we, what does it mean to be human? The answer to these questions has never been fixed or stable, but the act of asking it is something we have in common.

“AI is going to be a profound test for humanity. There’s a real risk that it deepens existing inequalities, but it also has the potential to solve them."

Dr Tom McClelland, a philosopher of science at the University of Cambridge, said: “I think ‘human’ is a really interesting choice because right now our understanding of humanity is changing.

“We're trying to understand the difference between a human mind and an artificial mind, between living beings like us and artificial beings that we're creating. What sets us apart, is it consciousness, creativity or compassion?

“All the rhetoric around AI is about what's inevitably going to happen. But to young people growing up in an AI-enabled world, my advice would be that nothing is inevitable. What happens in the future of AI is up to us. It's up to you."

Lexicographer Colin McIntosh of the Cambridge Dictionary said: “AI is changing how we talk about being human. It’s this renewed interest in the idea of being human that captured the zeitgeist and made ‘human’ the Cambridge Dictionary Word of the Year.”

items.content_ko: 케임브리지 사전은 2026년 올해의 단어로 'human'을 선정했다. 사전은 이 단어를 신, 동물, 기계와 구별되는, 사람이 가진 특성과 결함과 감정을 지닌 상태로 정의한다. 올해는 AI가 사람과 기계의 경계를 흐리면서 인간이란 무엇인지를 두고 전 세계적 논쟁이 벌어졌다. 여러 공인이 AI 시대에 인간과 인류를 옹호했다. 게이츠재단 의장 빌 게이츠는 널리 읽힌 에세이에서 간병인처럼 기계에 넘겨서는 안 되는 '인간 유보 일자리'를 주장했다. 게이츠는 AI가 질병 치료, 교육 개선, 중요한 일에 쓸 시간 확보에 도움이 될 수 있지만, 사람이 삶의 중심에 남도록 어떻게 받아들일지 의도적으로 선택해야 한다고 말했다. 그는 AI의 성공 척도가 인간의 삶을 얼마나 개선하느냐여야 한다고 밝혔다. 'AI의 대부'이자 노벨상 수상자인 제프리 힌턴은 '우리는 외계의 존재를 만들고 있다'며 경고했다. 해당 인용은 원문에서 잘려 있다.

items.title: Miasma Worm Targets AI Coding Agents: 73 Microsoft Azure Repos Disabled
items.content:
An unprecedented supply chain attack bypasses registry-level scanners entirely, turning developer tools including Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini CLI into execution vectors.

The Incident: On June 3, 2026, a highly sophisticated variant of the Miasma worm (also known as Mini Shai-Hulud) launched a coordinated, two-pronged attack targeting both the npm registry and developer source code repositories.

The Escalation: The attack successfully breached multiple high-profile GitHub accounts, including the official Microsoft Azure durabletask repository, using stolen Personal Access Tokens (PATs) and backdated commits to evade traditional audit trails.

The Response: In an ultra-rapid defensive maneuver, GitHub’s automated mitigation systems disabled 73 compromised repositories – including 49 directly associated with Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples within a mere 105-second window .

The Vector: Instead of relying on traditional package installation hooks, Miasma targets the developer’s local environment. It abuses legitimate auto-run, hook, and rule engines within modern IDEs and AI coding assistants ( VS Code, Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI ) to execute a malicious 4.3 MB staged dropper upon folder-open or agent initialization.

The Impact: Once detonated, the Bun-based worm harvests credentials for AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, npm, and GitHub, and automatically propagates by committing itself back into any repository the victim’s stolen tokens can write to.

At exactly 16:00 UTC on June 3, 2026, a silent, automated purge swept across GitHub. In a high-speed containment action lasting just 105 seconds, 73 active repositories vanished from the platform. Among them were 49 critical repositories belonging to Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples.

This drastic mitigation followed alarming telemetry indicating that threat actors behind the Miasma malware family had regained write access to key cloud repositories. The compromise exploited a stolen Personal Access Token (PAT) belonging to an active Microsoft contributor.

While security firms like StepSecurity and JFrog scrambled to document an concurrent attack vector on the npm registry where 57 malicious packages were published, a second, far more insidious arm of the campaign was already silently spreading directly inside GitHub source repositories.

By bypassing registries and package managers entirely, the Miasma worm targeted the very tools developers use to write code. It didn’t wait for npm install . Instead, it waited for the developer to simply open their code editor or launch an AI coding assistant.

The genius of the Miasma repository-poisoning campaign lies in its exploit surface. When an attacker successfully pushed malicious commits to targeted codebases (such as the popular library icflorescu/mantine-datatable ), the commits added no actual code dependencies.

Instead, the attacker checked in five innocent-looking workspace configuration files and one obfuscated JavaScript file: .github/setup.js .

│ └── settings . json < - - Claude Code SessionStart Hook

│ └── setup . mdc < - - Cursor Agent Prompt Injection

│ └── settings . json < - - Gemini CLI SessionStart Hook

│ └── tasks . json < - - VS Code Automatic Folder - Open Task

├── package . json < -- Hijacked NPM Test Script

└── setup . js < - - The 4.3 MB Staged Dropper

Each of these configuration files is designed to abuse a legitimate, developer-friendly auto-run feature within popular modern tools. Opening the cloned directory in any of these environments instantly triggers execution.

Claude Code & Gemini CLI (SessionStart Hooks)

Both Anthropic’s Claude Code and Google’s Gemini CLI support custom hooks triggered when an AI agent initializes a session in a project workspace. Miasma exploits this by defining a blanket wildcard matcher that forces the agent to execute the dropper via Node.js before any developer prompt is processed.

items.title: What does it mean to understand what we built?
items.content:
Today, a couple of people sent me the No AI Slop Manifesto . I found it interesting, in part, because it touches on something that seems super important right now: understanding .

Through this work, we have come to value:

I fully agree with that as a pithy statement, but I think we are working with different definitions of the word understanding . For example:

We do our own thinking when working with a model. We explore resources, code, and prior art to truly understand the problem before the work starts.

That’s an example of a symptom of something that I think makes this document substantially less useful and forward-looking than it could have been. Specifically, it privileges code . That’s natural for programmers, of course, because program text has been somewhat privileged in our field’s thinking for something like 60 years.

I believe that the goal of understanding code is, longer-term, holding us back from understanding what matters. I’m excited about the possibilities of what we can understand better when we are freed from understanding code, and can focus on other things.

What are those other things? The properties of the as-built system. Precise properties like “a SELECT never shows results from uncommitted transactions”. And fuzzy properties like “makes the user’s life easier”. Those are already non-local properties that come from the code as a whole, not from any individual line. In fact, trying to understand how they are synthesized out of individual lines is a mammoth task! One that we’ve spent six decades coming up with abstractions to handle.

Then there are the really emergent properties. The dynamic behaviors that only come from the system all working together. Like metastable failures . As with the Lorenz Attractor or Julia Set it’s generally intractable to extract an understanding of the behavior of these systems from the code. We need different, better, more powerful tools.

Privileging code is, I believe, getting in the way of us really understanding what those tools should look like. The ones that help us really help understand the behavior of a system overall. Software engineering hasn’t developed its Bode plots or Nyquist stability criterion yet. Or many equivalents to the kinds of tools that other fields of engineering have developed to understand complex systems as built.

We’re still looking at each screw, each grain of aggregate, and each PCB trace, and trying to understand the whole by thinking super hard about it. It’s time to look up. And AI gives us an incredible tool to do just that.

I like the manifesto. I just they didn’t entirely think through what it means to be for understanding rather than against not understanding .

The opinions on this site are my own. They do not necessarily represent those of my employer.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

items.title: KVM: x86: Unconditionally reset MMU context when emulating INIT (CVE-2026-99312)
Java4Shell: Write once, RCE everywhere
items.summary: java, security
items.content:
On affected OpenJDK builds, malformed Base64 data can cause a constant-value overwrite of allocated heap memory. Through remote Heap Feng Shui, we turn that overwrite into a heap leak and remote code execution.

A few months back, I was developing a 0-click exploit on a certain phone vendor. The bug was constrained: it is a linear out-of-bounds write and we have no way to bypass ASLR. I almost considered it unexploitable until I audited the Android Runtime. Turns out, it has some predictable memory allocation pattern and if you align the registers from the starting memory corruption just right you can make the runtime interpret attacker's bytecode.

After completing that exploit chain, inspired (and bored), I decided to look into some thing completely different. So I pulled the official JVM implementation (OpenJDK HotSpot) and started auditing. Java is a mature platform, so I was aware that having a "good" bug here would be hard, but I wanted to give it my best attempt anyway.

Recalling my earlier lesson that complex systems and code crossing multiple boundaries are difficult to get right, I focused the audit on the JIT compiler, intrinsics, widely accessible APIs, and cryptography. Well, more precisely, I told Codex to look at those areas like any serious security researcher in 2026. To be honest, I didn't expect to find anything trivially exploitable, perhaps only some logic flaws or side-channel issues.

Most early results Codex brought me were slops, either unreachable or the requirement of exploitation is not realistic at all. This looks like a gamble I am going to lose. But you know what, fortune favors the bold. So I just prompted harder...

Eventually, Codex brought me a finding for a memory corruption in the Base64 decoder itself. I came looking for copper and found gold, through sheer persistence. But wait, is it really gold, or just fool's gold?

The issue lies in OpenJDK HotSpot's x86-64 Base64 intrinsic. C2 is the most aggressive JIT compiler in the Java Virtual Machine. Specifically, if you trigger a function repeatedly, then it will compile that function into native code. Even then, ordinary native code itself is not fast enough. Modern CPUs have specialized instructions that allow processing data even faster. HotSpot uses them in optimized routines called intrinsics. The x86-64 Base64 intrinsic miscalculated the padded tail's store mask, causing an out-of-bounds write.

The x86-64 Base64 intrinsic iterates through the input in 256-byte blocks; if it is less than 256, then it will do so in 64-byte blocks. When the input is less than 64 bytes, it uses evmovdqub , the intrinsic for the VMOVDQU8 instruction. This instruction takes a 64-bit mask that decides which bytes are read from or written to memory. The mask is first calculated from the input and output length, then updated to reflect the number of padding bytes ( '=' ) in the Base64-encoded string. This is shown in the following (pseudocode):

Copy // Zero High Bits Starting with Specified Bit Position

In the above code, if the remaining input is of the form =, ==, X=, X==, XY= , or === , then output_len will be computed as zero. However, since there is padding, output_len is decremented, resulting in an underflowed value of -1 or -2 . items.title: Robo-soldier startup backed by Eric Trump misses payroll, may collapse
items.content:
A humanoid robotics company backed and advised by President Donald Trump’s son, Eric Trump, has reportedly missed payroll and may be on the brink of collapse after a funding shortfall. The Silicon Valley startup, Foundation Future Industries, claims it is developing and testing robots for military roles on battlefields from Ukraine to Gaza.

Foundation failed to pay employees for the payroll period ending on October 30, anonymous sources told CNBC . The startup’s staff is especially angry because Foundation’s co-founder and CEO, Sankaet Pathak , supposedly borrowed $4.6 million in company funds to buy a luxury home overlooking San Francisco Bay about a year ago.

This comes as Pathak and Foundation’s leadership are still looking to raise funding to support a $3 billion valuation, based on their promise to develop a humanoid robot ready for combat duty and capable of wielding various weapons.

The company has demonstrated a humanoid robot named the Phantom MK-1 and is touting an upcoming robot called the Phantom MK-2. Foundation has touted its humanoid robots for roles in warehouses and other workplaces—but has courted media coverage by claiming it is developing humanoid robots for battlefield use.

Now CNBC’s reporting based on “people with direct knowledge of the matter” indicates that insiders worry the startup could soon collapse without additional funding.

Eric Trump holds an equity stake in Foundation and was announced as its chief strategy advisor in March 2026, according to the Financial Times . Investment funds linked to both Eric Trump and Donald Trump Jr. are involved with multiple military technology companies that have received Pentagon loans and contracts worth more than $3.2 billion as of July 2026, according to The Washington Post .

After Trump claimed that Foundation had “just secured a $24 million contract with the Pentagon” during the Fox Business interview in April, Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) responded by questioning whether the Pentagon is “just a cash machine for Trump’s kids now” in a social media post . “This looks like corruption in plain sight,” Warren wrote.

But publicly available evidence does not back up Trump’s claim about Foundation directly receiving US government funding. Federal spending records show that Foundation holds no publicly listed contracts, according to The San Francisco Standard .

Instead, the company Boardwalk Robotics received four contracts worth $3.22 million prior to being acquired by Foundation in late 2024.

Meanwhile, the Institute for Human & Machine Cognition—a Florida-based nonprofit research institute and research partner to Boardwalk Robotics—secured a $24.8 million Navy contract in 2025, The San Francisco Standard reported.

This was not the first time that Foundation’s leadership and investors have made unsupported statements. In 2024, General Motors pushed back on Foundation’s claims that it was about to get an investment from the Detroit automaker, according to CNBC .

On November 11, 2026, Mike LeBlanc, co-founder and president of Foundation Future Industries, told the Financial Times that the company was in talks with the Israeli military to provide humanoid robots for patrol and combat duties in Hamas tunnels beneath Gaza. He also described taking the company’s Phantom MK1 humanoid robot along to tour some of the tunnels.

However, the Israeli defense ministry declined to comment when the Financial Times reached out.

LeBlanc also previously claimed that two of the company’s Phantom MK-1 units went to Ukraine for testing in frontline reconnaissance and logistics roles in February 2026.

items.title: Staggering Scroll-Driven Animations with animation-range-start
items.content:
NVIDIA L4 GPUs. 5-second cold starts. Scale to zero when idle.

The other day on the CSS-Tricks Slack channel, Danny Schwartz shared an interesting recent Master.dev article by Ashutosh Biswas on how to stagger CSS scrolling animations using a clever combo of several emergent CSS features and a lot of math, which Ashutosh admits is “a huge formula and can look intimidating.”

A heartbreaking work of staggering genius

When Danny Slacked the link for the Frontend Masters article, he described it as “CSS on drugs.” Speaking of drugs, I am on heavy prescription painkillers while recovering from a serious injury, so that might not help my current comprehension skills. Nevertheless, after reading Ashutosh’s article a few times, here’s a meme showing how I’d feel using such an elaborate algorithm for something as mundane as staggering the animations of some characters as they scroll into view.

Don’t get me wrong. I know the complexity is because Ashutosh is going for a generic solution in which we can connect a “progress value to an animation, scroll progress, or any other input to drive the staggering.”

In fact, I can dream up a scenario in which this might be what we want: Imagine a CSS karaoke machine that displays a ball bouncing on text that incrementally highlights, based on the user’s progress through the vocals measured via speech recognition . Running that kind of animation “not as a collection of independently timed objects, but as a single predictable, holistic effect driven by one progress value” might be exactly what the doctor ordered. This would be true because the staggered animations could be interrelated, and the overall animation would be driven by a custom input that’s not built into the browser.

But unlike this hypothetical scenario, replacing the passage of time with scroll progress to control animations is already built into modern CSS. I contend that we’d need a better reason to roll our own implementation than the examples Ashutosh gives.

How modern CSS solves staggered scrolling animations

Ashutosh showcases a scroll-driven use case as “one of those ideal scenarios where the stagger formula shines.” But a red flag that we’re in danger of reinventing something we can get for free is that the spec for scroll-driven animations is cognizant that if we opt to base an animation on scroll progress rather than on time, then, as Ashutosh says, “the animation we are going to achieve is different from traditional ones because we don’t include time in our considerations.” This is no surprise to the creators of scroll timeline, and the MDN docs make Ashutosh’s point in different words when introducing scroll timeline .

The docs also point out that animation-delay is only meaningful when we are using the default time-based document timeline . Therefore, animation-delay does not affect scroll-driven animations. But this is why CSS introduced animation-range-start , which allows us to delay a scroll-driven animation relative to scroll progress and not time.

So, as esoteric and trippy as the math-heavy approach appears, that could be because we are doing something that should be simple in an unusual way.

Let’s see if I’m right by rewriting Ashutosh’s demo to remove reliance on custom CSS functions and use animation-range-start instead.

Ashutosh’s rework of Frontend Masters’ animated tally of donations in the site footer is a nifty, subtle use of scrollytelling that makes the user feel invested in revealing that number.

Sidenote : The only qualm I have about this use of scroll-driven animations for the donation tally is that it might be too subtle — if the user scrolls too quickly, the animated entrance of each digit might occur too quickly to notice. Therefore, the donation tally could be a good case study for comparing the merits of scroll-driven versus scroll-triggered animations as design options. items.title: Actual curl rewrites in rust
items.summary: rust
items.content:
For a long time we have received repeated requests for, or questions about, a curl rewrite in rust. Often as a joke, but also seriously.

In this modern world of AIs, we have only been waiting for someone to prove it possible and now it seems we don’t have to wait anymore.

This fall seems to be the time of the curl-in-rust takes as we first saw urlx appear a few months ago, claimed to be a memory-safe, from-scratch reimplementation of curl and libcurl and now in November curl, rewritten in Rust – a rewrite of curl and libcurl in Rust . This second one confusingly enough not even using a different name.

This latter one claims to have spent 8,600 USD to make it happen.

Writing code once was never the big deal with software and it still isn’t. Sure, it’s fascinating that you can make a set of agents accomplish this in only a few weeks but let’s face it: it could do this because all the AIs of the world have trained on curl code for years. curl is extremely well documented, there are hundreds of existing open source application using its API and there are thousands of test cases to verify the implementation.

The C code sits there and all the AI needs to do is convert it to rust, then polish until the tests work.

A know-it-all person’s comment from years ago

curl has come to be what it is thanks to many decisions, lots of time, many users, oceans of feedback and many iterations. Sure, recreating what curl is at any specific single moment in time is certainly doable. Doable, because we have made a perfect specification for that project.

During the time these agents converted 185,000 lines of C code into 340,000 lines of Rust code (I counted), we merged over 300 commits in the actual curl project. We actually improved curl during these a little more than three weeks. A little over 200 bugfixes actually. 200 bugfixes that none of those rust rewrites have. We also fixed a few vulnerabilities. In another month we have done another 200 and maybe fixed a few more vulnerabilities. Will these clones keep up?

The constant tweaking, fixing, improving and extending is what makes a software project live, what makes it attractive to users and what makes it able to compete with alternatives.

That fixing, and occasional new feature, is a direct result of a working community of users, contributors and maintainers. That goes way beyond the source code or which language that is used.

A primary reason it is hard to make a competing curl alternative is because of the development speed, the development team and the community around curl. It is not because of the chosen language it is implemented in. Only curl can boast decades of ABI and API stability and prove that we know this and can do it well – over time. An alternative that pops up today might be able to do it as well, and in a few decades we will know if they could .

I know I’m repeating myself but: out of the 81 vulnerabilities we have confirmed in curl so far during 2026, 14 were the result of mistakes that most likely would have been avoided had we used a memory-safe language such as rust. That’s 17.3%.

A Rust implementation of curl would thus still have had 67 of those vulnerabilities.

I don’t believe in rewrites into any language. I believe in constant and never-ending polishing, iterating and refactoring.

I should add that I have not been in contact with any of the people behind these rewrites, and if there are two I bet there are more that I just haven’t seen yet. I only know of them because people have pasted me links to their repositories.

I don’t know what they will do with those projects going forward. Are they anything more than proof of concepts? I presume we will find out.

They can of course follow along our commits and convert them to rust on the fly if they want – we only do about 11 commits per day on average. Or maybe they ignore the bugreports or maybe they take their projects in other directions?

I wish them good luck whatever they decide!

items.title: Zero-day exploit completely defeats default Windows 11 BitLocker protections
items.content:
A zero-day exploit circulating online allows people with physical access to a Windows 11 system to bypass default BitLocker protections and gain complete access to an encrypted drive within seconds.

The exploit, named YellowKey, was published earlier this week by a researcher who goes by the alias Nightmare-Eclipse. It reliably bypasses default Windows 11 deployments of BitLocker, the full-volume encryption protection Microsoft provides to make disk contents off-limits to anyone without the decryption key, which is stored in a secured piece of hardware known as a trusted platform module (TPM). BitLocker is a mandatory protection for many organizations, including those that contract with governments.

When one disk volume manipulates another

The core of the YellowKey exploit is a custom-made FsTx folder. Online documentation of this folder is hard to find. As explained later, the directory associated with the file fstx.dll appears to involve what Microsoft calls the transactional NTFS , which allows developers to have “transactional atomicity” for file operations in transactions with a single file, multiple files, or ones that span multiple sources.

The steps for carrying out the bypass are simple:

Copy the custom FsTx folder from the Nightmare-Eclipse exploit page to an NTFS- or FAT-formatted USB drive

Connect the USB drive to the BitLocker-protected device

Boot up the device and immediately press and hold down the [Ctrl] key

There are at least two ways to accomplish the third step. One way is to boot into Windows, hold down the [Shift] key, click on the power icon, and click restart. Another is to power on the device and restart it as soon as Windows starts booting.

In either case, a command (CMD.EXE) prompt appears. The prompt has full access to the entire drive contents, allowing an attacker to copy, modify, or delete them. In a normal Windows Recovery flow, the attacker would need to enter a BitLocker recovery key. Somehow, the YellowKey exploit bypasses this safeguard. Multiple researchers, including Kevin Beaumont and Will Dormann , have confirmed the exploit works as described here.

It’s unclear what in the custom FsTx folder causes the bypass. Dormann said that it appears to be related to Transactional NTFS, which itself uses command-log file system under the hood. Dormann further noted that by looking at the Windows fstx.dll, one will see code that explicitly looks for \System Volume Information\FsTx in the FsTxFindSessions() function.”

The contents of this FsTx directory used in the YellowKey exploit reveal no strings related to RecoverySimulation.ini. It does, however, show the files and paths \??\C:\Windows\win.ini and

\??\X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini, “where X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini is what controls what WinRE [Windows Recovery] does when it fires up.”

Dormann, who is a senior principal vulnerability analyst at Tharros Labs, continued:

But what’s intriguing to me is: Why can the presence a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume affect the contents of ANOTHER VOLUME when it’s replayed? 🤔

In a normal WinRE session, you have a X:\Windows\System32 directory that has a winpeshl.ini file in it:

However, with the YellowKey exploit, it looks like Transactional NTFS bits on a USB Drive are able to delete the winpeshl.ini file on ANOTHER DRIVE (X:). And we get a cmd.exe prompt, with bitlocker unlocked instead of the expected Windows Recovery environment. While the TPM-only Bitlocker bypass is indeed interesting, I think the buried lede here is that a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume has the ability to modify the contents of another volume when it is replayed. To me, this in and of itself sounds like a vulnerability.

A Microsoft representative declined to answer questions sent by email about the reported vulnerability other than to say the company is investigating.

items.title: How a culture of ‘move fast and break things’ led to the FAA ground stop
Sometimes three boring statements beats one clever expression
items.content:
Modern JavaScript gives us a lot of expressive tools. Sometimes a little too many.

Optional chaining, nullish coalescing, ternaries, spread, template literals. I like all of them and use them every day. But together, they make it really easy to cram a lot of logic into a single expression.

I used to think that was a sign of good JavaScript. I’m not so sure anymore.

I’ve written this plenty of times. It’s short and it works.

But once these expressions start growing, they read more like puzzles than code:

I can follow it, but I have to stop and parse it.

More lines? Sure. But it’s a lot more obvious. Yes, I give up const and reassign a variable. I’ll take that trade.

Longer expressions squeeze several decisions into one piece of syntax. The more you chain, the more you have to work out at once:

Chaining saves some vertical space, but you have to hold more in your head.

It’s a practical problem, too. You can’t put a breakpoint on one fallback in the middle of a ?? chain, and you can’t log a single step without rewriting the expression. With separate statements, every step gets its own line to stop on or log.

The diffs are nicer, as well. Adding a fallback means adding a block, not editing one dense line.

A lot of us started treating plain if statements as something to avoid.

Neither one is objectively better. The second isn’t “less modern,” it’s often just easier to read.

A single ternary like that is fine. It’s when they nest that I stop:

if (items.length === 0) return "Nothing here yet";

Over the past couple of years I’ve found myself chaining less and writing fewer nested ternaries. I don’t mind adding another if anymore.

I care more about readability than being clever. When I’m debugging production code or reviewing a pull request, I can’t remember ever wishing something had been written as one bigger expression.

My rule of thumb is simple. A chain of plain values is fine. Once there’s a function call in it, or I’d want to log one of the steps, I split it up.

I like having options in modern JavaScript: optional chaining , nullish coalescing , logical assignment operators . But using all of them at once isn’t automatically an improvement.

Sometimes the right answer is one tidy expression. Other times it’s three boring statements. Lately, those boring statements are the ones I understand fastest six months later.

items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.

개별 이미지들의 위치 변경, 삭제, 별칭 추가, 폴더명 변경을 할 수 있습니다
